Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
45-year-old female housekeeper with 3–4 months of painful, itchy, cracked palmar skin—likely irritant contact dermatitis from occupational cleaning-chemical exposure.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive soreness, cracking, dryness, and intermittent itching of both palms since starting new housekeeping job 3–4 months ago; now painful enough to miss 3 workdays.  
• Associated symptoms: Occasional bleeding only when scratched; mild generalized leg dryness. Denies fever, GI, GU, or other systemic symptoms.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior eczema, asthma, or other skin disease.  
• PMH: Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Medications: Metformin; previously tried OTC E45 emollient and an antihistamine without benefit.  
• Allergies: None known.  
• Social / preventive: Hotel housekeeper; frequent chemical exposure, admits inconsistent glove use. Non-smoker. Alcohol ~2 pints beer/week. Hydration reportedly low. No other social risk factors noted.

Examination:
(Tele-visit; patient-reported findings)  
• Palms: Marked dryness with fissuring/cracks; tender; intermittent itch; no spontaneous bleeding.  
• No other exam or vital signs documented.

Impression:
Most likely diagnosis: Irritant contact dermatitis of the hands.  
Supporting evidence: Temporal relation to new cleaning job, direct palmar involvement, painful fissures > itch, lack of prior atopy, and inadequate glove protection.

Alternate considerations (lower likelihood):  
1. Allergic contact dermatitis to cleaning products—possible sensitization; itch present but pain predominates.  
2. Chronic hand eczema (atopic) —less likely given adult onset and clear occupational trigger.

Plan:
• Trigger avoidance: Strict glove use with all cleaning tasks.  
• Pharmacologic: Prescribed topical mid-potency corticosteroid cream plus high-emollient moisturizer; instruct to apply emollient liberally 3–4 times daily and steroid as directed for 10–14 days. Prescription sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy.  
• Education: Reviewed condition, importance of skin hydration, and avoidance of harsh chemicals.  
• Follow-up: Reassess in 1–2 weeks; earlier review if worsening, spreading, or no improvement.

Quality checks:

● Missing elements  
  – Vitals and in-person skin examination findings.  
  – Specific steroid name, strength, and dosing instructions.  
  – Complete medication list (metformin dose not recorded).  
  – Documentation of vaccinations, screening history.

● Conflicts between transcript and DDx  
  – None noted.

● Transcript quality  
  – Clear history; tele-visit limits objective exam; occasional minor audio gaps but overall understandable.
